Question 1
?

At which points on the curve y2+2x=2xy+2y−2 is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector i?

a
(−1,2) and (1,0)
b
(1,1) and (2,0)
c
(1,2) and (−1,0)
d
(−1,−2) and (1,0)
e
(1,−2) and (0,1)
Submit

decision.explanation: A tangent perpendicular to i is vertical. For F(x,y)=y²+2x−2xy−2y+2, this requires F_y=2y−2x−2=0, so x=y−1. Substitution into the curve gives y(2−y)=0, yielding (−1,0) and (1,2). At both points F_x=2−2y is nonzero, so the vertical tangent is well-defined.

after.problem: At which points on the curve ${y}^{2}+2x=2xy+2y-2$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2x & =2xy+2y-2 \\ {y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-2.$  

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y)j \\  & =(2y-2x-2)\,i-(2-2y)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((2y-2x-2)\,i-(2-2y)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2y-2x-2 & =0 \\ 2(y-x-1) & =0 \\ y & =x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x+1$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y & =-2 \\ (x+1)^{2}+2x-2x(x+1)-2(x+1)+2 & =0 \\ (x+1)^{2}-2x(x+1)-2(x+1)+2(x+1) & =0 \\ (x+1)^{2}-2x(x+1)-\cancel{2(x+1)}+\cancel{2(x+1)} & =0 \\ (x+1)^{2}-2x(x+1) & =0 \\ (x+1)(x+1-2x) & =0 \\ (x+1)(-x+1) & =0 \\ x & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=1$, we get $y=2$ and the corresponding point is $(1,2).$

- If $x=-1$, we get $y=0$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,0).$

Question 1

At which points on the curve y2+2x=2xy+2y−2 is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector i?

a
(−1,2) and (1,0)
b
(1,1) and (2,0)
c
(1,2) and (−1,0)
d
(−1,−2) and (1,0)
e
(1,−2) and (0,1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: y2+2x=2xy+2y−2y2+2x−2xy−2y=−2

If we set f(x,y)=y2+2x−2xy−2y, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=−2.

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows: t(x,y)=fy(x,y)i−fx(x,y)j

So, we calculate t(x,y):

t(x,y)=fy(x,y)i−fx(x,y)j=∂∂y(y2+2x−2xy−2y)i−∂∂x(y2+2x−2xy−2y)j=(2y−2x−2)i−(2−2y)j

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to i, we must have t⋅i=0.

t(x,y)⋅i=0((2y−2x−2)i−(2−2y)j)⋅i=02y−2x−2=02(y−x−1)=0y=x+1

Substituting y=x+1 into the equation of our curve gives:

y2+2x−2xy−2y=−2(x+1)2+2x−2x(x+1)−2(x+1)+2=0(x+1)2−2x(x+1)−2(x+1)+2(x+1)=0(x+1)2−2x(x+1)−2(x+1)+2(x+1)=0(x+1)2−2x(x+1)=0(x+1)(x+1−2x)=0(x+1)(−x+1)=0x=±1

Finally:

  • If x=1, we get y=2 and the corresponding point is (1,2).

  • If x=−1, we get y=0 and the corresponding point is (−1,0).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Points on a Curve at which the Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to a Given Vector
content.problem: At which points on the curve ${y}^{2}+2x=2xy+2y-2$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2x & =2xy+2y-2 \\ {y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-2.$  

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y)j \\  & =(2y-2x-2)\,i-(2-2y)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((2y-2x-2)\,i-(2-2y)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2y-2x-2 & =0 \\ 2(y-x-1) & =0 \\ y & =x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x+1$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y & =-2 \\ (x+1)^{2}+2x-2x(x+1)-2(x+1)+2 & =0 \\ (x+1)^{2}-2x(x+1)-2(x+1)+2(x+1) & =0 \\ (x+1)^{2}-2x(x+1)-\cancel{2(x+1)}+\cancel{2(x+1)} & =0 \\ (x+1)^{2}-2x(x+1) & =0 \\ (x+1)(x+1-2x) & =0 \\ (x+1)(-x+1) & =0 \\ x & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=1$, we get $y=2$ and the corresponding point is $(1,2).$

- If $x=-1$, we get $y=0$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,0).$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Vector to a Plane Curve
content.problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}y={y}^{2}+3.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(2,1).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y & ={y}^{2}+3 \\ {x}^{2}y-{y}^{2} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y-{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=3.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(2,1)={f}_{y}(2,1)\,i-{f}_{x}(2,1)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-{y}^{2})\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =({x}^{2}-2y)\,i-2xy\,j \\ t(2,1) & =({2}^{2}-2(1))\,i-2(2)(1)\,j \\  & =2\,i-4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $2\,i-4\,j.$

after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & =-y \\ 2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y)\,j \\  & =(-6y+1)\,i-4x\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $j,$ we must have $t\cdot j=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ ((-6y+1)\,i-4x\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -4x & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=0$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & =-y \\ 2({0}^{2})-3{y}^{2} & =-y \\ 3{y}^{2}-y & =0 \\ y(3y-1) & =0 \\ y & =0,\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the corresponding points are $(0,0)$ and $(0,\frac{1}{3}).$

content.problem: At which points on the curve $2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=-y$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $j?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & =-y \\ 2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y)\,j \\  & =(-6y+1)\,i-4x\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $j,$ we must have $t\cdot j=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ ((-6y+1)\,i-4x\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -4x & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=0$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & =-y \\ 2({0}^{2})-3{y}^{2} & =-y \\ 3{y}^{2}-y & =0 \\ y(3y-1) & =0 \\ y & =0,\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the corresponding points are $(0,0)$ and $(0,\frac{1}{3}).$
